questions.text:
QUESTION ONE: DC AND CAPACITORS

Stefan's car battery recently needed replacing, so he investigated new and used batteries in different situations. His car has a new battery with an EMF of 12.0 V and an internal resistance of 0.0500 Ω.

Explain the meaning of the term EMF.
questions.expectedAnswer: EMF is the voltage across the terminals of the battery when no current flows.

questions.text:
Stefan observes what happens to the voltmeter reading while opening and closing the switch.

Explain why the readings are the same or different.

Values and calculations are not required.
questions.expectedAnswer: When the switch is open, the voltmeter reads 12.0 V (no current, no voltage drop across internal...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: ONE of: switch open V = 12.0 V, switch closed V < 12.0 V, voltage/energy lost due to internal resistance, voltages are different. Merit: Complete answer including the reason why the voltmeter would read less than 12.0 V (via heat/energy/voltage drop or equation).

questions.text:
After long use the internal resistance of the 12 V battery increases to 0.500 Ω. The discharged battery is charged by a 24.0 V DC supply with a 15.5 Ω resistor in series.

Calculate the terminal voltage across the car battery.

Begin your answer by calculating the circuit current while it is being charged.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: ONE of: effective EMF = 12.0 V, attempt at Kirchhoff's voltage equation. Merit: I = 0.75 A, V = 11.7 V. One error in calculation. Excellence: V = 12.4 V. Working: +24 − 15.5I − 12 − 0.5I = 0. Effective EMF = 24 − 12 = 12 V. I = 12/16 = 0.75 A. Voltage across 15.5 Ω = 0.75 × 15.5 = 11.625 V. Terminal voltage = 24 − 11.6 = 12.4 V. OR Terminal voltage = 12 + (0.75 × 0.500) = 12.4 V.

questions.text:
Stefan connects a 12.0 V DC supply to a 0.140 F capacitor, two lamps, and a resistor, as shown below. The resistor and the lamps each have a resistance of 10.0 Ω.

Give an in-depth explanation of what Stefan would observe by comparing the brightness of lamps A and B:

- as soon as the switch is closed
- ten seconds after the switch is closed.
questions.expectedAnswer: Initially: Lamp A glows brightly as capacitor charges.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: ONE of: lamp A will glow initially, lamp A will stop glowing, lamp B will keep glowing, lamp B will be less bright. Merit: TWO of: lamp A glows brightly at start as capacitor charges; once fully charged current through A stops; lamp B will continue to glow; lamp A brighter than B because it has more current/voltage/power. OR lamp B glow less brightly as it shares voltage with the resistor. Excellence: ALL of: lamp A glows brightly at start as capacitor plates get charged; once fully charged, current through A stops so it stops glowing; lamp B will continue to glow AND lamp A will be brighter than B because it has more current/voltage/power. OR lamp B will glow less brightly because it has less voltage/current/power.

questions.text:
QUESTION TWO: ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION

Harry is experimenting with coils and magnets.

Harry measures an average EMF of 250 μV that is induced in a coil when the current in it changes from 10.0 A to 6.00 A in 0.400 s.

Calculate the self-inductance of the coil.

The coil has 25 turns and an area of 1.60 cm² (1.60 × 10⁻⁴ m²). This coil is inserted into a magnetic field of flux density 1.80 Wb m⁻², such that its plane is perpendicular to the lines of flux of the field. It takes 0.300 s for the coil to be placed in the magnetic field.

Calculate the EMF induced in the coil.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: ONE of: Δϕ = 2.88 × 10⁻⁴ Wb, Δϕ = 7.20 × 10⁻³ Wb, V = 9.6 × 10⁻⁴ V, V = 150 V, V = 240 V, V = 3.85 × 10⁻³ V. One error in calculation. Merit: V = 2.40 × 10⁻² V. Working: Δϕ = BA = 1.80 × 1.60 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.88 × 10⁻⁴ Wb (for one turn). V = −NΔϕ/Δt = 25 × 2.88 × 10⁻⁴ / 0.300 = 0.0240 V.

questions.text:
Harry then drops a bar magnet through a metal ring.

Explain why its acceleration will not be equal to 'g' = 9.81 m s⁻².

In your answer, include ideas about what happens when the magnet enters the ring, as well as when the magnet leaves the ring.
questions.expectedAnswer: As the magnet enters: changing magnetic flux induces a voltage and eddy current in the ring,...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: ONE correct statement of: downward acceleration < 9.81, changing magnetic flux, induced voltage/current, opposing magnetic field/flux is formed, it slows down. Merit: Changing flux linking the ring will cause an induced current which opposes the movement of the magnet. Acceleration < 9.81 because induced B/flux opposes the motion. Excellence: Includes explanation of what happens when the magnet enters as well as leaves the ring.

questions.text:
Harry next connects a 0.600 H inductor and a lamp whose resistance is 2.00 Ω, in series to a battery through a switch. Harry notices that the lamp takes some time to reach full brightness once the switch is closed.

Calculate the current through the lamp after 0.600 seconds.

Begin by calculating the time constant of the circuit.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: ONE of: I_max = 6.00 A, τ = 0.300 s, 1τ = 63% change. Merit: ALL of: I_max = 6.00 A, τ = 0.300 s, at τ I = 3.38 A. Correct method with minor error. Excellence: I = 5.18 A (or 5.19 A). Working: I_max = V/R = 12.0/2.00 = 6.00 A. τ = L/R = 0.600/0.300 = 0.300 s. 0.6 s is 2τ. I = I_max(1 − 1/e²) = 6.00(1 − 1/e²) = 6.00(0.8647) = 5.19 A.

questions.text:
QUESTION THREE: ALTERNATING CURRENT

Rachel is experimenting with AC circuits. She connects a 70.0 mH inductor with a soft iron core and a 40.0 Ω bulb in series to a 110 V_rms, 60.0 Hz supply.

Calculate the peak voltage of the power supply.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: V = 156 V. Working: V_peak = √2 × 110 = 155.6 ≈ 156 V.

questions.text:
Calculate the phase difference between the supply voltage and the circuit current, and state which one leads.

Begin your answer by showing that the reactance of the inductor is 26.4 Ω.
questions.expectedAnswer: θ = 33° (0.583 rad). Source voltage leads circuit current.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: MUST SHOW THAT: L = 0.070 and X_L = 26.4 Ω. θ = 33° (0.583 rad). Correct labelled vector diagram. Source voltage leads current. Merit: X_L = 26.4 Ω, θ = 33° (0.583 rad). Indication that source voltage leads current. Excellence: Complete answer with phasor diagram.

questions.text:
The inductor has a soft iron core.

Explain what Rachel would observe in the brightness of the lamp when she slowly removes the iron core from the inductor.
questions.expectedAnswer: Removing the soft iron core will decrease the inductance of the inductor.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: ONE of: L decreases, X_L decreases, Z decreases, I increases, brightness depends on power output, less back emf, brighter, smaller magnetic field/flux. Merit: L decreases therefore X_L will decrease. X_L decreases, Z decreases, so I will increase, causing the bulb to be brighter. Less back emf so greater voltage across bulb so its brighter. Excellence: Less back emf so greater voltage across bulb so its brighter because brightness depends on Power. Removing the iron core will decrease L, X_L decreases, Z decreases so I will increase. AND brightness depends on Power, so the lamp will be brighter because the current through the lamp increases. OR the voltage across the lamp will increase. Accept any justification with relevant power formula.

questions.text:
Rachel then reinserts the iron core and adds a capacitor to the circuit, in order to achieve resonance.

Explain why the reactance of the capacitor needs to be 26.4 Ω.

Begin your answer by describing what happens at resonance.
questions.expectedAnswer: At resonance, current is maximum and impedance is minimum (Z = R)
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: One correct statement: I is a maximum, Z = R, Z is a minimum, reactance of the capacitor cancels out reactance of the inductor. Merit: Any TWO achieved points. Excellence: ALL of: I is maximum, Z = R or Z is minimum, reactance of the capacitor cancels out, reactance of the inductor with reason (out of phase, equation or phasor diagram).
